title: "Ran with no errors" only covers the job's own log
explanation: Running `export-invoices.sh` by hand works fine, and its own cron log shows no failures either — the script's logic genuinely has no bug. But the actual failure surfaces one hop downstream: `sudo -u invoicer /opt/scripts/process-export.sh` prints `refusing to process /var/lib/invoicer/exports/last-export.txt: owned by root, not invoicer`. The export "succeeding" and the pipeline actually working are two different claims, and only the second one matters here.

title: The downstream rejection is a deliberate safety check, not a bug in it
explanation: `process-export.sh` refuses to touch any file it doesn't itself own — a defensive measure so the pipeline never processes something an unrelated principal (even root) could have planted there. `ls -l /var/lib/invoicer/exports/last-export.txt` confirms the concrete gap: the file is owned by `root`, not `invoicer`. Understanding that this check is intentional matters, because the fix is to satisfy it, not to weaken or bypass it.

title: Whoever cron runs a job as owns everything that job writes
explanation: `cat /etc/cron.d/export-invoices` shows the job line runs as `root`: `* * * * * root /opt/scripts/export-invoices.sh ...`. The user field in a crontab entry isn't just "who's allowed to run this" — every file the job creates is owned by that same account. The export script's logic was never wrong; only which identity cron invoked it under was.

title: Fix the identity at the source, not the file after the fact
explanation: `chown`-ing the existing file to `invoicer` would only patch this one output — the very next minute's run, still executing as `root`, would immediately re-create a root-owned file and undo the fix. The real correction is in the job definition itself: `sudo sed -i 's/^\* \* \* \* \* root /* * * * * invoicer /' /etc/cron.d/export-invoices` (or editing the user field directly) changes which account produces the file going forward, permanently.

title: Verify the whole chain, not just the export step
explanation: Re-running the export the way cron now will (`su -s /bin/sh -c /opt/scripts/export-invoices.sh invoicer`) and then `sudo -u invoicer /opt/scripts/process-export.sh` confirms both halves: the fresh file is owned by `invoicer`, and the downstream consumer accepts it. When a pipeline's own script runs clean but a later stage rejects its output, check which account actually ran it, not just whether it ran.
